rationale: Start with a broad mid-temperature scouting gradient to elute all 10 compounds and map the full retention window without undue risk of truncation. This gives a first read on where peaks cluster, whether any are near-unretained or held to the final hold, and how much room there is to narrow the window later.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the priority is to cut t_last below 10 min while keeping the peaks inside the gradient window. The first run suggests the elution window is roughly phi_e 0.11 to 0.41, so a narrower, shorter gradient ending at 0.65 should preserve resolution while substantially reducing run time.

The only lost score is the 6/7 pair, which fell from full resolution to R 1.39 when the gradient was made steeper, while t_last is already just under 10 min. A small increase in tG at the same window should restore that pair to at least 1.5 with only a modest increase in analysis time.

The 6/7 pair is the only issue at the 10 min gradient, so change temperature rather than slope to seek a selectivity improvement while keeping t_last near or below 10 min. Raising T should also shorten the run slightly, and this test will show whether that critical pair is temperature-sensitive.

The critical 6/7 pair is strongly temperature-sensitive in the wrong direction, so revert to 40 C and instead narrow the gradient window slightly to make the local slope shallower around the elution region. This should improve the 6/7 separation while keeping the last peak close to 10 min.

At phi1 0.60 and 10 min all pairs are resolved, but the score is now limited only by t_last being 0.71 min too long. Shortening tG one step should pull the last peak close to or below 10 min while likely keeping the critical 6/7 pair near the 1.5 threshold.

The tradeoff is now clear: shallower gradients fix the 6/7 pair but push t_last above 10 min, so test lower temperature to improve that pair’s selectivity while keeping the successful 0.60 window. This run will show whether cooling can restore or improve 6/7 resolution enough to offset any added retention.

Temperature changes hurt selectivity, so return to 40 C and instead shift the whole gradient window upward while keeping the same width and tG as the current best method. Since the first peak is still well retained, a higher phi0 should shorten the run and may move the critical mid-cluster onto a more favorable part of the gradient without making it steeper.

You already have the maximum CRF, so now probe whether the method can be made faster without losing full resolution. Shortening tG one step at the same successful window and temperature is the cleanest way to test whether the critical 6/7 pair stays at or above 1.5.

The 8 min gradient was too steep for the 6/7 pair, so keep tG at 10 min and narrow the window slightly from the strong method at injection 8. This should preserve the beneficial higher phi0 while making the gradient shallower around the critical cluster and may still keep t_last under 10 min.

Injection 8 is already perfect on CRF, but there may be room to make the run even faster while staying fully resolved by shifting the whole window slightly higher. The first peak is still comfortably retained, so increasing phi0 by one step may shorten the method and could keep the critical 6/7 pair above 1.5 without changing gradient width.

With injection 11, the first peak is getting close to the dead-time region yet all pairs are still fully resolved, so test a slightly higher overall window while preserving the 0.50 gradient span. This may shorten the method further without sacrificing the critical 6/7 pair, and the slightly higher phi1 helps avoid pushing the last peak past 10 min.

Injection 12 pushed the window too high and weakened the 6/7 pair, while injection 11 was fully resolved with margin. Split the difference by keeping phi0 at the successful 0.15 but raising phi1 one step to see if the last peak can be pulled earlier while preserving full resolution.

The best methods sit right on the edge for the 6/7 pair, and simple temperature decreases at 10 min shifted selectivity but also altered which pair was critical. Testing the successful higher-phi0 window with a shorter gradient at lower temperature will map whether cooling can recover selectivity enough to allow a faster fully resolved method than the current 10 min optimum.

Lower temperature made selectivity markedly worse, so check the opposite direction at the strongest fully resolved window from injection 11. This will confirm whether 40 C is truly optimal or whether a hotter run can keep all pairs resolved while trimming time further.

Temperature excursions are clearly detrimental, so stay at 40 C and test whether a narrower window can rescue the critical 6/7 pair at the faster 8 min gradient. Compared with the failed 0.10/0.65/8 run, this keeps the advantageous higher phi0 but makes the gradient shallower, which may allow a faster fully resolved method.

At 40 C, narrowing the window to 0.15–0.60 gives extra resolution margin but t_last is slightly too long; at 0.15–0.65, heating to 45 C badly hurt 6/7. Testing 45 C with the narrower 0.15–0.60 window checks whether that added slope margin can absorb the temperature-induced selectivity loss and still yield a faster fully resolved method.

A hotter 10 min run collapsed the 6/7 pair, so this single follow-up checks whether the temperature effect is mainly slope-sensitive by compensating with a shallower gradient at the same window. If 6/7 remains poor even at 12 min, that effectively rules out 45 C and confirms the current 40 C optima.

Forty degrees is clearly the only useful temperature, and the best region lies between the fully resolved 0.10/0.65 and the too-fast 0.15/0.70 family. Testing a slightly wider upper window from the injection-8 optimum probes whether the last peak can be shortened further while still holding the critical 6/7 pair at or above 1.5.

To shorten the run while protecting the critical 6/7 pair, go in the opposite direction from the failed higher-phi1 trials and narrow the window from the fully resolved 0.15/0.65 method. This should further flatten the gradient around the clustered peaks, and the already high phi0 may still keep t_last near 10 min.

The remaining unexplored corner near the two perfect methods is to raise phi0 further while keeping the successful upper limit of 0.65 and a narrower width than injection 12. This tests whether a higher starting composition can shorten the run without the selectivity loss seen when both phi0 and phi1 were pushed upward together.

Injection 21 is very close to perfect but just misses full credit on the 6/7 pair; narrowing the window one step should make the gradient shallower and may push that pair above 1.5. Although t_last may rise somewhat, it has 0.69 min of headroom under 10 min, so this is a worthwhile final refinement around the current near-optimum.

The best score is already 1.000, so use one of the last injections to test whether a modest temperature decrease at the known optimum window preserves full resolution or reveals a different selectivity regime. This is the only nearby variant not yet checked around the best method, and it will confirm whether 40 C is truly the unique optimum.

With only two injections left and 1.000 already achieved, use one to bracket the temperature sensitivity more decisively at a proven perfect window. This low-temperature check can reveal whether a very different selectivity pattern emerges that might support a different fast optimum, while still staying in a known safe composition window.

For the final injection, target the only near-perfect method that still has room for improvement: injection 21 missed full credit only because the 6/7 pair was at R 1.45. Lengthening that exact window one step should lift 6/7 above 1.5 while keeping t_last comfortably under 10 min, offering a last chance at another 1.000 method.
